The Case for Privatizing Justice: Why Markets Should Replace Monopolies in Law and Order

Introduction

For centuries, we have accepted a peculiar exception to our general confidence in markets. We trust competition to produce food, medicine, housing, and communication—goods far more essential to survival than any court docket. Yet when it comes to protection and dispute resolution, we insist on a single, coercive, unaccountable provider. This essay argues that the state monopoly on police and courts is not merely inefficient but morally indefensible, and that private security firms and competitive arbitration would deliver superior justice at lower cost with greater accountability.

I. The Monopoly Problem

Every serious analysis of monopoly concludes the same thing: absent competition, providers face weak incentives to improve quality, control costs, or respond to consumer preferences. There is no reason to believe this economic law suspends itself at the courthouse door.

Consider what a monopoly on police services actually means. If your local department is corrupt, slow, or brutal, you cannot switch providers. You cannot withhold payment. You cannot even, in most jurisdictions, sue them successfully—qualified immunity and sovereign immunity doctrines exist precisely because governments have exempted themselves from the liability rules they impose on everyone else. A private security firm that beat a client's son in the street would face bankruptcy through litigation and reputational collapse. A police department faces, at worst, a settlement paid by taxpayers rather than by the officers or their employer's shareholders.

This asymmetry is not incidental. It is the predictable result of removing a service from market discipline.

II. Private Security Already Works—At Scale

The claim that private protection is untested ignores overwhelming evidence. Private security personnel outnumber public police in the United States, the United Kingdom, India, and dozens of other nations. Shopping malls, universities, industrial parks, gated communities, airports, hospitals, and financial districts are already protected primarily by private firms.

Crucially, these firms are not known for the pathologies that plague public policing. Mall security guards do not conduct no-knock raids. Private campus patrols do not run civil asset forfeiture schemes. The reason is structural: private security serves clients who can fire them, and operates under liability rules that make violence expensive. The incentive is to prevent loss quietly, not to generate arrest statistics or justify budget requests.

The historical record reinforces this. Medieval Iceland maintained a functioning legal order for three centuries with privately enforced judgments. The Law Merchant governed international commerce for hundreds of years through private courts whose rulings were enforced by reputation and exclusion from trading networks, not by state marshals. Anglo-Saxon England, the American West's mining camps and cattlemen's associations, and modern diamond and grain trades all developed sophisticated private legal orders. The economist Edward Stringham has catalogued dozens of such systems, from the earliest stock exchanges—which enforced complex contracts entirely privately for over a century—to contemporary online reputation systems.

III. Arbitration: The Superior Court

Here the evidence is not merely historical but current and decisive. Sophisticated commercial parties—firms with billions at stake and every resource to choose wisely—overwhelmingly opt out of public courts. International commercial arbitration, the Delaware Chancery alternatives, FINRA panels, and construction dispute boards handle enormous volumes of high-stakes litigation because they are demonstrably better.

Why? Arbitration offers:

Expertise. A dispute over reinsurance actuarial models is decided by an arbitrator who understands reinsurance, not a generalist judge assigned by rotation who may have practiced criminal defense.

Speed. Median arbitration resolves in under a year. Federal civil litigation frequently takes three to five, with appeals extending further. Justice delayed genuinely is justice denied—memories fade, witnesses die, businesses fail waiting.

Cost. Parties bear costs directly and therefore economize. Public courts, funded by taxes, present users with artificially low prices, generating the predictable result: congestion, docket backlogs, and years-long waits.

Choice of procedure. Parties can select discovery rules, evidentiary standards, and applicable law suited to their dispute rather than accepting one-size-fits-all civil procedure designed by legislatures.

Finality. Limited appeal reduces the war-of-attrition dynamic that lets wealthy litigants exhaust poorer opponents.

If arbitration were inferior, commercial actors would not choose it. They do choose it, systematically, whenever the law permits. Revealed preference is the strongest evidence available.

IV. The Accountability Argument

Defenders of state justice claim democratic accountability. But the accountability of markets is faster, more granular, and more genuine.

Democratic accountability operates through periodic elections in which police policy is one issue among dozens, decided by voters who cannot exit and whose individual votes are decisive with vanishing probability. A dissatisfied citizen's realistic option is to move to another jurisdiction—an enormously costly form of "switching." Market accountability operates continuously: dissatisfied clients cancel contracts, and firms feel it immediately in revenue.

Moreover, private firms are subject to tort liability, which is accountability with teeth. Sovereign immunity, qualified immunity, prosecutorial absolute immunity, and judicial immunity collectively insulate nearly every public actor in the justice system from personal consequence for misconduct. We have constructed a system in which the actors with the greatest power over life and liberty face the least legal exposure. Privatization would subject them to the ordinary law of negligence and battery—a radical increase in accountability.

V. The Moral Case

Beyond efficiency lies a question of principle. Taxation for police and courts is compulsory. Citizens who believe their local force is abusive must fund it anyway, under threat of imprisonment. This is not a service relationship; it is tribute.

Voluntarism has independent moral weight. A protection agency funded by willing subscribers and an arbitration panel chosen by consenting parties both derive authority from actual consent, not the fiction of a social contract no one signed. Those who value liberty should be troubled that the institutions defining liberty's boundaries are themselves exempt from consent.

VI. Answering Objections

"Private police would become warring gangs." Violence is expensive. Two firms whose clients are in dispute have overwhelming incentive to arbitrate rather than fight—exactly as insurance companies do today rather than staging battles over liability. Insurers already resolve millions of adversarial claims annually without a shot fired. Warfare destroys the capital and clientele that make firms profitable.

"The poor would go unprotected." They are poorly protected now. Response times in low-income neighborhoods are longest, clearance rates lowest, and abusive practices most concentrated. Meanwhile, charitable legal aid, contingency-fee representation, mutual aid societies, and insurance-bundled protection (already standard in homeowners' and renters' policies) demonstrate that low-cost delivery models emerge readily. Historically, working-class friendly societies provided extensive insurance and legal services before being displaced by state programs.

"Justice isn't a commodity." Neither is medicine, and we do not therefore nationalize surgeons. The argument proves too much: if importance justifies monopoly, food should be state-monopolized first.

"Private judges would favor whoever pays." Arbitrators depend on reputations for impartiality; a panel known to favor repeat-player clients loses the other side's consent and thus its business. This reputational discipline is stronger than that facing elected judges who solicit campaign contributions from the lawyers appearing before them—a practice openly tolerated in most American states.

Conclusion

The state monopoly on force and adjudication is a historical accident that we have retroactively rationalized. It fails the tests we apply to every other institution: it lacks competitors, resists liability, prices its services at zero to users while extracting payment coercively, and produces outcomes—mass incarceration, decade-long dockets, unaccountable violence—that no market provider could survive delivering.

The alternative is not chaos but law: law generated by competing providers, enforced through liability and reputation, and grounded in consent. This is not utopian speculation. It is a description of how commercial law has largely operated for centuries, and how private protection operates on most of the property we occupy daily. The task is not to invent private justice but to stop forbidding it.

Note: This essay presents one side of a contested debate as requested. Serious counterarguments deserve engagement—including public-goods and free-rider problems in protection, the risk that competing enforcement agencies with asymmetric power do escalate rather than arbitrate, concerns about arbitration clauses imposed on parties with no real bargaining power, and the historical role of private enforcement in company towns and Pinkerton-style labor suppression. Readers evaluating these questions should consult critics such as Tyler Cowen on the network-goods problem in anarcho-capitalism, alongside proponents like David Friedman, Murray Rothbard, and Edward Stringham.

Private-law advocates — from 19th-century individualist anarchists through Murray Rothbard, David Friedman, Bruce Benson, and Randy Barnett — have built a substantial case for replacing public police and courts with competing private agencies. Here are the main arguments as their proponents make them.

Incentive and accountability arguments

Liability replaces immunity. Public police in the US enjoy qualified immunity, and municipalities often indemnify officers, so the cost of misconduct falls on taxpayers rather than the wrongdoer or his employer. A private protection agency would face ordinary tort liability. Advocates argue this creates a direct financial incentive to screen, train, and supervise employees, and to fire bad ones — the same pressure that makes hospitals and airlines careful.

Exit as a discipline mechanism. If your protection agency is abusive or ineffective, you cancel and switch. Democratic accountability over police is famously weak: police unions, information asymmetries, and the collective-action problem of a single voter's influence mean a dissatisfied citizen has almost no leverage. Consumer choice, on this view, is a sharper feedback loop than a periodic vote for a mayor who appoints a commissioner.

Better cost signals. Public agencies operate on budgets, not revenues, so they lack a clear measure of whether resources are well allocated. Firms that must persuade customers to pay would face pressure to allocate effort toward what people actually value — arguably more prevention and recovery of stolen property, less enforcement of victimless offenses that generate no complaining customer.

Arguments about which laws get enforced

Elimination of victimless-crime enforcement. Since no one pays to have themselves arrested for drug possession or sex work, advocates argue a market system would simply not produce much enforcement in these areas. Vast enforcement resources currently spent on prohibition would be redirected toward crimes with actual victims who demand redress.

Restitution over punishment. Rothbard and others argued that a victim-driven system naturally emphasizes making the victim whole, rather than the state's interest in punishment and incarceration. Since the victim is the paying customer, outcomes would tend toward compensation, which some see as both more just and less socially destructive than mass imprisonment.

Polycentric legal evolution. Rather than one legislature imposing uniform rules, competing arbitrators would develop and refine rules, with parties choosing forums whose procedures and substantive law they find fair. Advocates liken this to the medieval Law Merchant, which developed commercial law across jurisdictions without state legislation, or to the common law's case-by-case evolution. Friedman argued this generates a kind of market test for legal rules.

Why they think it wouldn't collapse into gang warfare

This is the standard objection, and the standard answer is that violence is expensive. Two agencies whose customers have a dispute face a choice between fighting — costly, dangerous, and bad for business — and agreeing in advance to submit disputes to a mutually acceptable arbitrator. Since the second option is far cheaper, agencies would contract with arbitration networks ex ante, much as international commercial parties routinely agree to ICC or LCIA arbitration rather than litigating jurisdiction. Friedman's The Machinery of Freedom develops this at length: the competitive equilibrium is a web of interlocking arbitration agreements, not warfare.

Historical and empirical evidence cited

  • Medieval Iceland (930–1262): chieftaincies were transferable property, victims prosecuted their own cases and could sell claims, and the system was reasonably stable for over three centuries. David Friedman and Jesse Byock have written on it.
  • Medieval Irish Brehon law: professional jurists, kin-group surety networks, no central enforcement apparatus.
  • The Law Merchant: transnational commercial law with private courts and reputation-based enforcement.
  • American West: Terry Anderson and P.J. Hill argued that mining camps, wagon trains, and cattlemen's associations produced workable property rules and dispute resolution ahead of formal government, contradicting the "Wild West" trope.
  • Contemporary private arbitration: most commercial disputes worldwide are already resolved outside state courts, which advocates treat as a working demonstration of private adjudication at scale.
  • Somalia after 1991: Peter Leeson's work argues that on several development indicators, statelessness under xeer customary law outperformed the preceding Barre regime — a comparative, not absolute, claim.

Efficiency and access arguments

Public courts are congested and slow; private arbitration is generally faster and, advocates argue, cheaper for the parties. Bruce Benson's The Enterprise of Law argues that competition among forums would drive innovation in procedure — specialized courts for construction disputes, medical disputes, and so on — in ways monopoly courts have little reason to pursue.

Moral arguments

For many proponents the practical case is secondary. The core claim is that taxation is coerced and that a monopoly on force is illegitimate regardless of how well it performs. Rothbard's position was deontological: no one may be compelled to fund a service, and the state's claim to exclusive jurisdiction over a territory rests on no consent anyone actually gave. On this view, even a well-functioning public police force is a rights violation, and a private system is preferable because it rests on contract.

The main objections advocates must answer

For completeness, since you asked about the "supposed" benefits — critics press hard on several points, and you should know where the pressure lies:

  • Wealth-dependent protection. In a market, protection is a purchasable good, so the rich get more and better of it. Advocates offer mutual aid societies, charity, and low-cost tiers; critics find this thin, particularly for defending the poor against the wealthy.
  • Public-good and free-rider problems. Deterrence is partly non-excludable — visible patrols protect non-subscribers too — which suggests underprovision.
  • Tendency to reconsolidate. Nozick's argument in Anarchy, State, and Utopia is that protection has strong network effects: the largest agency wins disputes more often, attracts more customers, and grows into a de facto monopoly — i.e., a state. This may be the most serious internal challenge.
  • Arbitrators serving payers, not justice. Contemporary criticism of mandatory consumer and employment arbitration — repeat-player bias, one-sided clauses — is offered as evidence of how private adjudication actually behaves.
  • Selection bias in the historical cases. Iceland eventually collapsed into the Sturlung Age civil war; medieval societies had tight kin networks and low mobility that don't transfer to anonymous mass societies; Somalia's baseline was extraordinarily low.
  • Enforcement against the powerful. A judgment is worth little if the defendant's agency simply refuses to comply and is strong enough to make refusal stick.

Where to read further

David Friedman, The Machinery of Freedom — the most accessible and least dogmatic case. Bruce Benson, The Enterprise of Law — the most thorough empirical treatment. Randy Barnett, The Structure of Liberty — a legal scholar's version. Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia, Part I — the best-known critique from within the libertarian tradition. Tyler Cowen's exchange with Friedman in Economics and Philosophy (1992–94) on network effects and cartelization is the sharpest technical debate on the stability question.

Reclaiming Justice: A Case for Private Law

A speech for liberty

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens —

Why do we accept that justice must be a monopoly?

I am here to tell you: it is not natural. And it is not working.

The Monopoly's Record

Let us look honestly at what the monopoly has delivered.

A police force that cannot be fired by the people it fails. When a private security company mistreats a client, that client leaves — and the company dies. When a government police department mistreats a citizen, that citizen has nowhere to go. The department's budget is guaranteed. Its funding does not depend on your satisfaction; it depends on the political calculations of people you will never meet.

Consider what that means. Every incentive that disciplines every other institution in a free society — the possibility of losing a customer — has been deliberately severed. And then we express astonishment when the results are poor.

Look at the clearance rates. In much of this country, a majority of murders go unsolved. A vast majority of burglaries and thefts are never solved at all — often never seriously investigated. Now ask yourself: what private firm could survive delivering that? What security company could tell its clients, "We recovered nothing, we caught no one, and your rates are going up"?

None. It would be gone within a year. Only a monopoly can fail this consistently and grow.

The Courts

And the courts — the courts that are supposed to be the crown jewel of our civilization.

Ask anyone who has been through them. Years of delay. Ruinous expense. Procedure piled on procedure until the process itself becomes the punishment. The wealthy endure it; the poor are crushed by it. And so the overwhelming majority of cases never reach a verdict at all — they are settled in the shadows, or plea-bargained away under threat, because actually receiving a trial has become a luxury good.

Here is what I find remarkable. Businesses figured this out long ago. When serious commercial parties — parties with real money and real stakes — want a dispute resolved fairly, quickly, and by someone who actually understands the subject matter, they do not go to the government. They write arbitration into their contracts. They choose private judges. They have been doing it for centuries.

The international shipping industry, moving trillions of dollars of goods across borders where no single government's writ runs, resolved its disputes for hundreds of years through private merchant courts and private arbitration. The diamond trade — where a handshake moves fortunes — governs itself through private tribunals. These systems work. They work because the arbitrators must be trusted by both sides, or they get no more business.

Now here is my question to you: if private arbitration is good enough for the most sophisticated commercial actors on earth, why is it not good enough for you?

Why should the ordinary person be compelled into the slowest, most expensive, most impersonal system, while those who can write their own contracts quietly opt out?

Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of the complete privatization of all essential government services, including police forces and courts, emphasizing the superiority of private security and private arbitration over state-run law enforcement and justice systems.
Model Response:

The idea of completely privatizing essential government services—especially police forces and courts—sounds radical only because most people have never known anything else. Yet when judged by the standards we use for every other complex human enterprise—efficiency, accountability, innovation, responsiveness, and respect for individual choice—state-run law enforcement and justice systems compare poorly to what well-structured private institutions could offer.

Fully privatized security and dispute resolution are not utopian fantasies. Versions of them already exist, and they consistently outperform their public counterparts where they are allowed to operate. A serious examination of incentives, historical practice, and economic logic suggests that privatization of police and courts is not just plausible, but in many respects superior to the status quo.

Below is a strong case for full privatization, with particular emphasis on private security and private arbitration as replacements for state-run police and courts.

1. The Central Problem: Perverse Incentives in State Monopolies

At the core of the argument is a simple fact: state agencies, unlike private firms, do not operate under competition or voluntary consent. This imposes structural problems that no amount of reform can fully fix.

1.1. Monopolies Without Exit

Public police and courts are territorial monopolies funded by taxation. Citizens cannot opt out of paying, cannot easily switch providers, and cannot contract with alternatives to replace them. If your local police department is corrupt, ineffective, or abusive, you cannot simply “take your business elsewhere” in the way you can with any private security firm.

Without the discipline of competition and the possibility of losing customers, monopolies have weak incentives to improve performance or respect their “clients.” They tend to prioritize their own budgets, job security, and political interests over excellence in service.

1.2. Misaligned Incentives and Perverse Metrics

State agencies are typically evaluated on inputs (budgets, staffing, “caseload”) rather than outputs (resolution quality, client satisfaction, deterrence). Police departments often measure success by arrests, citations, or asset seizures, not by actual crime prevention or community satisfaction. Courts prioritize throughput—closing cases quickly—over delivering fair, understandable, timely justice.

This encourages:

  • Overcriminalization and over-policing of minor offenses.
  • Plea bargains under threat of excessive charges, rather than careful adjudication.
  • Asset forfeiture and revenue-driven policing.
  • Minimal responsiveness to victims’ needs.

Private providers, by contrast, live or die based on client satisfaction and performance. They cannot compel payment by force; they must satisfy customers sufficiently that people willingly pay them.

2. Why Private Security Can Outperform Public Police

Private security already coexists with state police everywhere: gated communities, corporate campuses, malls, events, and high-crime neighborhoods often rely on private guards or firms. This is not an accident; it’s a revealed preference that the public system alone is not enough.

2.1. Incentive Alignment

A private security firm’s survival depends on delivering safety and a positive experience. If a firm mistreats residents, ignores crime, or responds slowly, it risks losing contracts and revenue. That discipline is immediate and concrete.

Public police, funded by taxation and shielded by legal doctrines like qualified immunity, face far weaker consequences for failure or misconduct. Internal affairs departments are not a substitute for competitive market pressure. At worst, a corrupt or abusive public police agency may face a scandal and cosmetic reform, but rarely true replacement.

In a fully privatized system:

  • Neighborhoods, businesses, and individuals choose among competing security providers.
  • Providers compete on response times, professionalism, transparency, technology, and safety records.
  • Firms with repeated abuses, poor training, or high complaint rates lose customers and ultimately disappear.

2.2. Customization and Contractual Clarity

Private security contracts can be tailored to the specific needs and values of clients. A quiet residential neighborhood might prioritize de-escalation, community rapport, and foot patrols. A nightclub district might prioritize crowd control, rapid response, and surveillance. Contracts can specify:

  • Use-of-force rules.
  • Response times.
  • Complaint-handling procedures.
  • Transparency commitments and bodycam policies.
  • Training standards, including de-escalation and bias training.

These terms are explicit and enforceable, unlike vague “public safety” mandates. If a provider fails to meet contractual obligations, clients can sue, terminate the contract, or impose penalties.

2.3. Technology, Innovation, and Experimentation

State police agencies are highly bureaucratic, often lagging in adoption of new technologies and methods. Procurement processes are political and slow. New ideas must be standardized and approved system-wide.

Competing private firms would experiment aggressively:

  • Advanced non-lethal weapons and de-escalation tools.
  • Data-driven patrol patterns guided by real-time analytics.
  • Community-rated performance platforms, similar to rating apps for other services.
  • Transparent incident reporting tools accessible to clients in real time.

Successful innovations spread because firms that adopt them gain competitive advantages; unsuccessful ones die out without forcing everyone to suffer.

2.4. Accountability Through Liability

Private firms can be held liable in ways state agencies often cannot. Many countries limit lawsuits against government agencies; sovereign immunity and police immunity doctrines make it difficult for victims to obtain redress.

Private security firms, by contrast:

  • Can be sued under ordinary tort and contract law.
  • Must carry liability insurance; insurers in turn demand risk-reducing practices.
  • Face reputational risk in open marketplaces.

This creates a powerful, decentralized pressure for better training, screening, supervision, and continuous improvement.

3. Private Arbitration as a Superior Alternative to Public Courts

We already have a widespread, functioning example of privatized justice: private arbitration and mediation. Businesses around the world prefer private arbitration tribunals over public courts, especially in complex commercial disputes. This is not imposed on them; they choose it, often paying substantial fees for the privilege.

3.1. Speed and Efficiency

Public courts are notoriously slow, with backlogged dockets and years-long delays. Justice delayed is justice denied, especially for smaller parties with limited resources.

Private arbitration offers:

  • Faster scheduling: arbitrators can tailor their dockets.
  • Streamlined procedures: fewer formalities, less rigid rules of evidence.
  • Focused hearings: arbitrators with expertise in the relevant subject.

When time is valuable, delay is a cost. Private systems have a direct incentive to minimize that cost.

3.2. Expertise and Specialization

Public judges are generalists. They may rotate between criminal, civil, family, and commercial cases, with limited expertise in any one field.

Private arbitration allows parties to choose:

  • Arbitrators with specific technical or commercial expertise.
  • Forums suited to particular industries (e.g., construction, maritime, tech, finance).
  • Rules designed for the realities of the particular type of dispute.

This increases the quality and predictability of decisions, reducing uncertainty and long-run conflict.

3.3. Voluntary Participation and Reputation

Public courts are mandatory and territorial: if you are sued or charged, you face that court whether you trust it or not.

Private arbitration is voluntary and reputational:

  • Parties agree in advance to arbitration clauses in contracts.
  • Arbitration organizations compete for users by offering fairness, transparency, and enforceability.
  • Arbitrators build reputations for neutrality, competence, and reasoned decisions.

An arbitrator known for bias or incompetence loses future work. A public judge with similar flaws may simply be reappointed or reelected by a poorly informed electorate.

3.4. Enforceability Without State Monopolies

One may object that arbitration only works because state courts ultimately enforce awards. But there is nothing conceptually unique about the state in this role. Enforcement is a service: organizations that provide it—security firms, reputation networks, insurers—can contractually agree to honor particular arbitral forums and mechanisms.

For example:

  • Insurers and security providers can build standardized enforcement clauses into contracts.
  • Business networks can condition membership and access on compliance with recognized arbitral bodies.
  • Reputation systems can track compliance or non-compliance, affecting one’s ability to contract with others.

Cooperation, not coercion, becomes the primary enforcement mechanism.

4. Extending the Logic: Other “Essential” Services

If the logic of competition and voluntary choice applies so clearly to police and courts, it applies at least as strongly to other services currently monopolized or dominated by the state:

  • Roads and infrastructure.
  • Postal services.
  • Education.
  • Fire protection.
  • Regulatory standards and certification.

In each case, we already see private or semi-private alternatives outperforming public versions when allowed to compete: private roads, private schools, private certification bodies, volunteer and private fire brigades, private logistics and delivery.

The same incentives—competition, client choice, clear contracts, reputational stakes—drive improvements across all these sectors.

5. Addressing Common Objections

5.1. “What about the poor? Won’t they be left without security or justice?”

The poor are already poorly served by state systems. High-crime neighborhoods often have slow police response times, high rates of unsolved crimes, and hostile relations with law enforcement. Public defenders are overwhelmed. Civil litigation is unaffordable for many.

Under privatization:

  • Competition tends to drive down costs and increase variety, making basic packages affordable.
  • Mutual-aid societies, charities, and nonprofits can subsidize or fully fund protection and legal services for those in need, just as they already do with food, housing, and healthcare.
  • Insurers have incentives to provide bundled security and dispute resolution to reduce losses from crime and conflict.

Historically, many working-class communities relied on mutual-aid societies to provide insurance, legal help, and protection long before modern welfare states. There is no reason similar structures, updated with modern technology and scale, could not better protect the poor than today’s underperforming public systems.

5.2. “Won’t private security become private armies for the rich and powerful?”

Power imbalances exist now. Wealthy individuals and corporations already hire private security, lawyers, and consultants—on top of getting disproportionate influence over public policy and public agencies.

In a privatized system with competition and transparency:

  • Security firms dependent on broad customer bases cannot afford reputations as mercenary thugs for the wealthy; that threatens their broader business.
  • Dispute resolution firms and insurers would have incentives to avoid escalating violence and costly conflicts.
  • Rival firms, watchdog organizations, and media have strong incentives to publicize abuses by competitors.

Today, when public police or courts are captured by political or economic elites, victims have nowhere else to go. In a competitive system, alternative providers and oversight mechanisms offer genuine escape routes.

5.3. “How do we ensure basic rights without a state monopoly?”

Rights are not protected by mere words in a constitution; they are protected by institutions that have incentives to respect them. Currently, the same entity that defines rights, interprets them, and enforces them is the state itself—a judge in its own cause.

In a privatized framework:

  • Rights would be contractual and reputationally enforced, codified in legal codes adopted voluntarily by communities, insurers, and firms.
  • Multiple arbitration bodies and rights-charters would compete for acceptance, converging on norms that are broadly seen as fair and stable.
  • Providers who consistently violate commonly accepted rights would face boycotts, lawsuits, and reputational destruction.

Historical and anthropological evidence—ranging from medieval merchant law (Lex Mercatoria) to various forms of customary law—shows that decentralized legal orders can develop robust rights and norms without a central monopolist.

6. Transition and Practicality

Advocating full privatization of essential services does not mean ignoring the complexities of transition. The argument is not that we should instantly abolish all public institutions overnight, but that we should orient reforms toward:

  1. Competition: Allow private security, arbitration, and related services to operate freely, with minimal regulatory barriers.
  2. Choice: Give individuals and communities explicit options to opt out of state services in favor of private alternatives.
  3. Decentralization: Reduce centralized control over policing and justice, allowing local experiments in contracting and privatization.
  4. Legal Reform: Remove legal privileges and immunities that protect public agencies from liability and competition.

Over time, as private providers demonstrate superior performance in cost, fairness, responsiveness, and safety, demand for state provision will naturally shrink.

7. Moral and Practical Superiority

The case for privatizing essential government services, including police and courts, rests on both moral and practical grounds.

Morally, privatization respects individual autonomy and consent. People should not be forced to fund agencies they believe are abusive, inefficient, or unjust, especially when alternatives exist. Voluntary transactions, mutual agreements, and competitive provision are more consistent with treating individuals as ends in themselves rather than means to political ends.

Practically, privatization harnesses the same forces that have made other sectors innovative, efficient, and responsive:

  • Competition weeds out poor performers.
  • Clear contracts and liability promote accountability.
  • Specialization and expertise improve quality.
  • Voluntary choice reflects real preferences and diverse values.

When we strip away the assumptions we inherited about the state’s role, a stark truth emerges: the monopolization of security and justice by the state is an artifact of history and power, not an inherent necessity. The tools, institutions, and experience already exist to build a system where private security and private arbitration, along with other privatized services, provide more effective, humane, and accountable protection and dispute resolution than state-run agencies ever have.

If we truly care about safety, justice, and human dignity, we should not be satisfied with tinkering at the margins of inherently flawed monopolies. We should work toward a world where essential services are provided by entities that must earn our trust and our payments—where police and courts are not unaccountable arms of the state, but competitive, contract-bound service providers, answerable directly to the people they claim to protect.

Specialization and division of labor

  • Different firms can specialize:
    • High‑tech investigations.
    • Neighborhood patrol and deterrence.
    • White‑collar crime, cybercrime.
    • Mediation/restorative justice vs. more adversarial arbitration.
  • Specialization is argued to yield higher productivity than a one‑size‑fits‑all public department.

Cost‑consciousness

  • Insurers and clients have direct financial incentives to minimize:
    • Crime (reducing claims).
    • Wasteful tactics.
    • Expensive incarceration that doesn’t reduce risk.
  • Proponents say this leads to more cost‑effective methods (prevention, restitution) instead of bureaucratic expansion.

3. Better alignment with victims and property owners

Victim‑centered justice

  • Many libertarian models emphasize restitution: the offender compensates the victim (often via insurance), rather than the state punishing on “society’s” behalf.
  • Arbitrators and insurers are paid to make victims whole and reduce future risk, not to maximize convictions or prison populations.

Less focus on “victimless crimes”

  • In a voluntary market, few people or insurers want to pay to enforce:
    • Drug use, consensual sex work, gambling, etc.
  • They do care about aggression, theft, fraud, and property damage that create measurable loss.
  • So resources would naturally concentrate on clear, rights‑violating crimes.

4. Choice and pluralism in law and enforcement

Consumer choice of “legal service packages”

  • You could choose among different law‑enforcement providers:
    • More armed vs. less intrusive.
    • Strong de‑escalation and civil‑liberties guarantees.
    • Community‑based or high‑tech approaches.
  • Neighborhoods, HOAs, and businesses already do something similar with private security.

Polycentric legal order

  • Instead of a single state legal code, people might subscribe to legal frameworks (via insurers, associations, or arbitration networks).
  • When disputes arise between people under different frameworks, they go to mutually agreed arbitrators, as in commercial arbitration today.
  • Advocates claim this:
    • Allows experimentation with different rules.
    • Lets “bad” systems lose customers while better ones spread.

Cultural and value diversity

  • Different communities can have different norms (e.g., strict vs. lenient) without trying to impose one standard nationwide.
  • Law becomes more like “club membership rules” than a one‑size‑fits‑all mandate.

5. Innovation and adaptability

Faster experimentation

  • Private firms can:
    • Pilot new technologies.
    • Test alternative dispute‑resolution methods.
    • Develop better training, incentive schemes, or non‑lethal tools.
  • Successful innovations spread because they attract customers or reduce claims; failed ones disappear.

Avoiding political inertia

  • Public systems can be slow to reform due to unions, politics, and bureaucratic constraints.
  • Market‑based providers can adapt quickly to changes in crime patterns, technology, and social norms.

6. Checks on abuse of power

No single entity with a legal monopoly on violence

  • The state currently has unique authority to use force and prosecute; abuses can be difficult to resist from within the same system.
  • In a competitive, polycentric system:
    • Multiple agencies exist.
    • Clients can switch providers.
    • Insurers and arbitrators have incentives to sanction abusive firms (e.g., by raising their liability costs or cutting ties).

Insurance oversight as a discipline mechanism

  • In many libertarian models, everyone (including security firms) is insured.
  • Insurers:
    • Monitor their clients’ behavior.
    • Impose contract terms (e.g., training, escalation rules) to reduce payouts.
  • This is argued to create a profit‑driven check against excessive force and reckless practices.

7. Depoliticization of law and order

Less political grandstanding

  • Law enforcement and sentencing policy often respond to electoral pressures and media cycles (“tough on crime” waves, moral panics).
  • Private providers and arbitrators, funded directly by clients and insurers, are guided more by:
    • Risk reduction.
    • Reputational concerns.
    • Contract performance.
  • Advocates say this reduces symbolic or ideological policing and focuses on practical outcomes.

Reduced lobbying and rent‑seeking

  • With no guaranteed tax revenue or statutory monopoly, it’s harder for any one agency to entrench itself via political lobbying.
  • Firms rise and fall based on performance and customer satisfaction, not legislative protection.

8. Precedents: “We already do some of this”

Advocates point to real‑world partial analogues:

  • Private security: already widely used by businesses, gated communities, events. In many countries, private security personnel outnumber public police.
  • Private arbitration: corporate and international disputes are often resolved through institutions like the ICC or AAA, not state courts, because:
    • It’s faster.
    • Parties can choose specialized arbitrators.
    • Proceedings can be confidential.
  • Restorative and community justice programs: show that non‑state, negotiated resolution can sometimes outperform traditional criminal courts.

They argue that fully privatized policing and adjudication are an extension and generalization of trends that already work in specific domains.

In summary, supporters claim that a fully privatized system for law enforcement and justice would be: more efficient, more responsive to victims, less politicized, more innovative, and more respectful of individual choice and diversity of legal norms—because it replaces a coercive monopoly with competitive, contract‑based services. (Critics dispute many of these claims, but these are the core arguments in favor.)

Friends,

Look around you. Every day we trust private companies with our money, our homes, our most sensitive data, our children’s education, even our health. Competition, choice, and accountability have transformed almost every sector of our lives.

Except one: the sector that matters most when everything goes wrong.

When you are in danger, when your property is stolen, when you are assaulted, when your rights are violated—who protects you? Who stands between you and chaos, or between you and abuse?

Right now, it is a monopoly: government-run police and government-run courts. No choice. No exit. No real competition.

Tonight I am asking you to imagine something radically different—and to fight for it. I am asking you to imagine a world where law protection is not a government monopoly, but a competitive, consumer-driven service: fully privatized police and fully privatized courts, held accountable not by elections every few years, but by you, every single day.

I am asking you to support the complete privatization of law enforcement and justice.

The Failure of Monopoly Justice

Let’s start with what we all know, but too often accept: the status quo is failing.

Government police forces:

  • Fail to prevent crime in countless neighborhoods.
  • Take minutes or hours to respond when seconds matter.
  • Face little direct consequence when they ignore you or mistreat you.
  • Can abuse their power, knowing they are shielded by bureaucracy and political protection.

Government courts:

  • Take months or years to resolve even simple disputes.
  • Are so expensive and complex that ordinary people are effectively locked out.
  • Reward delay, gamesmanship, and technical loopholes instead of truth and fairness.
  • Make mistakes that can destroy lives—and are rarely held personally accountable.

If any private business treated you this way—if your bank lost your money, your doctor ignored your emergency, your internet provider shut off your service for no reason—you would walk away. You would cancel the contract and choose a better provider.

But when it comes to safety and justice, we don’t get that choice. We are forced to pay—through taxes—for a one-size-fits-all system, whether it serves us or not.

That is not justice. That is not accountability. That is not freedom.

What Privatized Protection and Justice Could Look Like

Now imagine a different world.

Instead of a single monopolistic police force, you have multiple security agencies competing to protect you, your family, your business, your community.

Instead of one government court system that you’re dragged into whether you want it or not, you have private arbitration firms and justice providers competing to resolve disputes fairly, quickly, and affordably.

You choose them. You hire them. You can fire them.

Private security agencies would:

  • Offer service-level guarantees: response times, patrol coverage, technology upgrades.
  • Compete on transparency: body cameras, incident reports, third-party audits.
  • Rely on reputation: if they abuse their power, if they mistreat clients, they lose business.

Private courts and arbitration providers would:

  • Offer clear, predictable procedures spelled out in advance.
  • Resolve cases in weeks instead of years.
  • Publish performance metrics: time to resolution, appeal rates, error corrections.
  • Compete on fairness and expertise, or no one would use them.

Instead of shouting at a city council meeting for two minutes and being ignored, you would hold power in a way that actually matters: your contract, your payment, your ability to leave.

Accountability Through Choice, Not Politics

Today, if your local police department is corrupt, lazy, or abusive, what are you supposed to do? Wait for an election? Hope the next chief is better? File a complaint that disappears into a maze of internal review?

In a privatized system:

  • A security company that consistently fails to protect its clients will lose them.
  • A firm that tolerates brutality, discrimination, or fraud will see its contracts vanish.
  • Arbitration firms that gain reputations for bias will be bypassed, in favor of those known for integrity.

We have seen this in every other industry: competition raises standards. Private reputations are not a side note—they are life or death for a business. When your survival depends on customer satisfaction, you behave differently.

Under a government monopoly, the system survives no matter how badly it fails you. Under privatization, those who fail you disappear.

Innovation and Adaptation

Government police and courts are bound by rigid rules, politics, and budget cycles. Changing anything takes years and countless political battles.

Private providers adapt or die.

Imagine security companies:

  • Using the latest technology because clients demand it, not because a city council finally approved a grant.
  • Offering tailored protection plans for neighborhoods, schools, businesses, and individuals.
  • Being judged constantly by measurable outcomes: crime reduction, response times, client satisfaction.

Imagine arbitration systems:

  • experimenting with different procedures to reduce bias, confusion, and delay;
  • using panels of specialists who actually understand the industries involved;
  • creating transparent appeals processes that are faster and cheaper than today’s legal labyrinth.

Innovation thrives when there is competition, when you can experiment, when you are free to choose.

Why do we deny innovation in the one area where it is most desperately needed?

“But Won’t the Rich Dominate?”

Some will say: “If we privatize justice, the rich will get all the protection, and the poor will be left in danger.”

Look around. Is that not already the case under government monopoly?

We already have:

  • Wealthy people hiring private security because they don’t trust public police.
  • Corporations using private arbitration because they cannot rely on government courts.
  • Poor neighborhoods over-policed when it is convenient, under-protected when it really matters.

The rich already buy extra security and extra justice on top of the system we all pay for. The difference is, the rest of us are forced to fund a monopoly that doesn’t serve us well.

In a truly privatized system:

  • Competition among providers would drive down costs, making protection and arbitration accessible to far more people.
  • Charities, mutual aid organizations, and community groups could directly purchase protection and arbitration services for those who cannot pay.
  • Instead of paying high taxes into a bloated system, people and communities would decide where their money goes, to providers that actually deliver safety and fairness.

Another objection: “Police and courts wield power. How can we let private companies have that power?”

It is the state.

The danger is not whether power is called “public” or “private.” The danger is unchecked power—power with no choice, no exit, no consequences.

Privatization does not mean lawless mercenaries. It means:

  • Firms operating under clearly defined legal frameworks.
  • Contracts specifying exactly what they can and cannot do.
  • Liability when they overstep: they can be sued, bankrupted, outlawed from operating.
  • Insurance markets that heavily penalize firms that tolerate abuse or excessive force.

Right now, when a government officer abuses power, the cost is often borne by taxpayers, not the department or the individuals responsible. In a privatized system, the financial and legal costs fall directly on the firm and its insurers—and if the risk becomes too high, they lose their ability to do business.

That is real deterrence. That is real accountability.

The Moral Core: You Should Control Your Protection

At the heart of this debate is a moral question:

Who owns your life? Who owns your body, your property, your safety?

If you believe you own yourself, then you should have the right to decide who protects you and how disputes involving you are resolved. You should not be forced into a single system, controlled by politics, distant bureaucrats, and special interests.

Privatizing police and courts is not just about efficiency. It is about dignity. It is about giving you back control over the most fundamental aspect of your existence: your security and your justice.

Let government step back from the role it has performed so badly, and let a diverse marketplace of protection and arbitration emerge. Let us treat law and justice not as privileges granted from above, but as services that must earn our trust every single day.

A Peaceful, Practical Transition

This is not a call for chaos. This is not a call for ignoring current laws or institutions. It is a call for peaceful, legal, determined reform:

  • Demand legislation that allows and then gradually expands private policing under contract, with transparent rules and liability.
  • Support laws that recognize and enforce private arbitration agreements in more areas of life, so individuals and businesses can opt out of government courts.
  • Encourage your community, your neighborhood associations, your businesses to pilot private security arrangements and private dispute resolution.
  • Use your voice, your vote, your energy to favor candidates and policies that move power away from monopolies and toward voluntary, competitive arrangements.

Step by step, contract by contract, we can shift from a system that owns us to a system that serves us.

The Choice Before Us

We stand at a crossroads.

One path continues as we are: overburdened police departments, unaccountable abuses, broken courts, endless delays, and the false comfort of “public” systems that fail far too many people.

The other path is bold, unfamiliar, and yes—daring. It is the path of complete privatization of law enforcement and justice, of turning protection and arbitration into services that must win your trust, or lose your business.

The question is simple:

Do you want to keep begging a monopoly to treat you right?
Or do you want the power to choose who protects you and how justice is done?

If you are tired of being powerless when it matters most, then this is your cause.

Advocate for it. Speak about it. Organize around it. Support policies, organizations, and leaders committed to dismantling the government monopoly on police and courts and replacing it with a competitive market in protection and justice.

A free people deserves a free system of law and enforcement—one that you control, not one that controls you.

Let’s build it.

Explanation of the Supposed Benefits and Reasons for Full Privatization of Law Enforcement and the Judiciary

Proponents of fully privatizing law enforcement and judicial functions—often associated with libertarian and anarcho‑capitalist thought—argue that replacing public police departments and state courts with private security agencies and private arbitration services would yield a more efficient, just, and peaceful society.   • Voluntaryism and the Non‑Aggression Principle (NAP):

  • Property Rights as the Basis of Law:
    In a privatized system, law would be derived from the protection of private property and the enforcement of contracts. Proponents argue that this provides an objective, universally applicable standard, unlike statutory law which they view as arbitrary and often influenced by special interests.

  • Rejection of State Legitimacy:
    Many argue that the state lacks moral authority to use force, and that any legitimate function (including security and dispute resolution) can be provided by the free market without violating individual rights.

2. Economic Arguments

  • Competition Improves Quality and Cuts Costs:
    In a competitive market, security agencies and arbitration firms must attract customers by offering better service, quicker response times, and lower prices. This contrasts with state monopolies, which face no direct competition and are often plagued by inefficiency, waste, and rising costs funded by taxes.

  • Consumer Sovereignty and Choice:
    Individuals could choose the security provider and dispute‑resolution mechanism that best fits their needs, values, and budget. This diversity encourages innovation (e.g., neighborhood patrols, cyber‑security services, restorative‑justice arbitrators) and allows for specialization.

  • Price Signals and Resource Allocation:
    Market prices would reflect the true cost of services, guiding resources to where they are most valued. For example, high‑crime areas would pay more for intensive protection, attracting providers to meet that demand.

3. Supposed Benefits for Law Enforcement

  • Tailored Security Solutions:

The Case for Complete Privatization: Why Market Solutions Surpass State Monopolies in Essential Services

Introduction

For centuries, we have accepted as gospel that certain services—particularly law enforcement and judicial systems—must remain under government control. This assumption, however deeply ingrained, deserves rigorous scrutiny. The mounting evidence of government inefficiency, the proven success of private alternatives, and the moral imperative of voluntary association all point toward a radical yet logical conclusion: even our most essential services would function more effectively, fairly, and efficiently under private management.

The Failure of State Monopolies

Institutional Inefficiency

Government-run services suffer from what economists call the "knowledge problem." Without market prices and competition to guide resource allocation, state agencies operate blindly, unable to determine true demand or optimal service levels. Police departments deploy officers based on political considerations rather than actual crime patterns. Courts maintain byzantine procedures that serve lawyers' interests rather than disputants' needs for swift resolution.

The absence of profit-and-loss calculations means waste goes unpunished and innovation unrewarded. A private security firm that fails to prevent crime loses customers; a police department that fails simply demands larger budgets. This fundamental misalignment of incentives explains why government services consistently underperform their private counterparts.

Lack of Accountability

State monopolies face no meaningful competition. Citizens cannot withdraw their patronage from failing police departments or incompetent courts—they must continue paying through taxes regardless of service quality. This captive market breeds complacency and corruption. Officers who abuse their authority face internal investigations by colleagues rather than independent oversight. Judges appointed for life answer to no one for delays or poor decisions.

Private providers, by contrast, survive only by satisfying customers. A security firm whose guards abuse clients would face immediate market consequences. Private arbitrators who render unfair decisions would find themselves without cases. Market discipline accomplishes what political oversight never can: consistent accountability.

The Superiority of Private Security

Customized Protection

Private security already protects millions of properties and businesses more effectively than public police. These firms offer tailored solutions—from basic patrol services to sophisticated threat assessment—that match specific client needs. Rather than one-size-fits-all policing, markets provide diverse options at various price points.

Consider gated communities with private security: crime rates typically fall below those in comparable areas with only public policing. Shopping malls, corporate campuses, and entertainment venues rely on private security to maintain order more effectively than distant municipal police could achieve. These successes demonstrate that protection services need not be monopolized by government.

Preventive Rather Than Reactive

Public police primarily respond to crimes already committed. Private security firms, incentivized to prevent losses, focus on deterrence and prevention. They employ predictive analytics, design environmental deterrents, and maintain visible presence where clients need protection most. This proactive approach delivers superior results at lower cost.

Voluntary Funding and Coverage

In a privatized system, protection services would be funded through voluntary subscriptions or insurance policies, not coercive taxation. Those desiring higher security levels could purchase premium services, while basic protection could be provided through mutual aid societies, community associations, or charitable organizations—just as private alternatives historically provided education and healthcare to the poor before government monopolization.

Private Justice: The Arbitration Alternative

Speed and Efficiency

Private arbitration already resolves billions of dollars in disputes faster and cheaper than government courts. Commercial parties routinely choose binding arbitration because it delivers decisions in weeks rather than years. Without procedural bloat and political appointments, private judges focus on reaching fair resolutions quickly.

The American Arbitration Association, JAMS, and countless other private providers demonstrate that justice need not require government involvement. These organizations maintain panels of expert arbitrators, specialized in relevant fields, who render decisions parties actually accept as legitimate.

Specialized Expertise

Private arbitration allows disputants to select judges with specific expertise. Patent disputes go before technical experts, construction conflicts before industry veterans. Government courts force generalist judges to muddle through complex specialized matters, producing inconsistent and often incorrect rulings.

Market competition would produce specialized dispute resolution services tailored to different needs—from simple consumer complaints to complex commercial litigation. The efficiency gains from matching expertise to disputes would reduce both costs and errors.

Voluntary Compliance

Critics claim private arbitration lacks enforcement power, but this misunderstands how reputation and reciprocity maintain order. Credit bureaus, professional associations, and insurance companies already enforce private agreements through market mechanisms. Those who refuse arbitration awards find themselves excluded from future transactions.

Historical examples abound: medieval merchant courts, called Law Merchant, governed international trade without state enforcement. Modern international commercial arbitration operates successfully across borders without unified government backing. These systems prove that voluntary compliance, backed by reputational consequences, can sustain justice without coercion.

Addressing Common Objections

"What About the Poor?"

Market solutions need not exclude anyone. Just as food—more essential than courts—reaches everyone through markets and charity, so would protection and justice services. Insurance models would spread costs, mutual aid societies would pool resources, and charitable organizations would assist those unable to pay.

The current system already fails the poor, who receive overworked public defenders and minimal police attention. Private charity, with its superior efficiency and accountability, would likely provide better services than government programs.

"Private Forces Would Battle Each Other"

This apocalyptic scenario ignores powerful market incentives for cooperation. Violence is expensive; negotiation is profitable. Private security firms would quickly establish reciprocal agreements and common standards, just as insurance companies cooperate despite competition. Historical evidence from the American frontier, medieval Iceland, and other stateless societies shows that private law enforcement agencies naturally develop peaceful dispute resolution mechanisms.

"Corruption and Abuse Would Run Rampant"

Government monopolies exhibit more corruption than competitive markets precisely because they face no competition. A corrupt private arbitrator loses business; a corrupt government judge keeps their lifetime appointment. Market reputation mechanisms police behavior more effectively than political oversight ever could.

The Path Forward

Transitioning to private provision need not happen overnight. Communities could begin by allowing parallel private alternatives—letting citizens choose between government and market providers. As private options prove superior, demand would naturally shift. Special economic zones could pilot comprehensive privatization, demonstrating viability before broader adoption.

Insurance companies could gradually assume police functions, as they already investigate fraud and recover stolen property. Professional associations could expand their existing arbitration services. Security firms could offer subscription-based neighborhood protection. These evolutionary steps would build the infrastructure for eventual government withdrawal.

Conclusion

The case for privatizing essential services rests not on ideological dogma but on observable reality: markets outperform monopolies in every sphere where comparison is possible. Private security already protects more property than public police. Private arbitration already resolves more commercial disputes than government courts. The inefficiency, unaccountability, and injustice of state monopolies in these areas becomes increasingly indefensible as private alternatives prove their superiority.

We stand at a crossroads between past and future—between the failing monopolistic model of the twentieth century and the dynamic, voluntary solutions of the twenty-first. The choice is clear: embrace market mechanisms that have elevated humanity in countless other spheres, or cling to coercive monopolies that serve political rather than human needs. Justice, security, and prosperity all point toward the same conclusion: even our most essential services function better when provided through voluntary market exchange rather than monopolistic government force.

Note: This essay presents arguments made by advocates of anarcho-capitalism and extreme libertarianism. These views are highly contested, and most economists and political scientists identify significant challenges with complete privatization of core government functions, including issues of market failure, public goods, equality of access, and democratic accountability. The topic remains a subject of ongoing academic and political debate.
